parts.stem: Prove the trigonometric identity \(\tan3\theta=\frac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}\) using the compound angle formula.
parts.hint: tan 3θ = tan(2θ + θ), then use the tan 2θ formula.

steps.explain: Write \(3\theta=2\theta+\theta\) and use the compound angle formula.
Let \(t=\tan\theta\) and use \(\tan2\theta=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}\).
Multiply numerator and denominator by \(1-t^2\).
Simplify.

parts.answer: \(\tan3\theta=\tan(2\theta+\theta)=\frac{\tan2\theta+\tan\theta}{1-\tan2\theta\tan\theta}\); substitute \(\tan2\theta=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}\) (t = tan θ) and multiply top and bottom by \(1-t^2\): \(\frac{2t+t(1-t^2)}{1-t^2-2t^2}=\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}\).

keyPoints.note: Split 3θ = 2θ + θ.

parts.stem: Hence find expressions for the exact values of the solutions to the equation \(\frac{3x-x^3}{1-3x^2}=\sqrt3\).
parts.hint: Set \(x=\tan\theta\) with \(-\frac\pi2<\theta<\frac\pi2\), use part (i), then list the tangent solutions that fit the resulting range of \(3\theta\).

steps.explain: Put \(x=\tan\theta\), choosing the unique \(\theta\in(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2)\) for each real \(x\). By part (i), the left side is \(\tan3\theta\).
Tangent has period \(\pi\), so \(3\theta=\frac\pi3+k\pi\). Since \(-\frac{3\pi}{2}<3\theta<\frac{3\pi}{2}\), only \(k=-1,0,1\) are possible.
Take the tangent of each angle. Since \(\tan(7\pi/9)=\tan(-2\pi/9)\), this matches option D.

keyPoints.note: With x = tan θ, the left side is tan 3θ by part (i).

parts.hint: Turn the equation into a cubic and use the product of roots.

steps.explain: Rearrange the equation into a cubic.
Its three roots are the values from (ii).
Product of the roots of \(ax^3+bx^2+cx+d\) is \(-\frac da\).

parts.answer: \(\frac{3x-x^3}{1-3x^2}=\sqrt3\Rightarrow3x-x^3=\sqrt3-3\sqrt3x^2\Rightarrow x^3-3\sqrt3x^2-3x+\sqrt3=0\). Its roots are the three values from (ii), so their product is \(-\frac da=-\sqrt3\).

keyPoints.note: The three tangents are the roots of the cubic from (ii).

Triangle for \(\beta\): \(\cos\beta = \dfrac{3}{5}\) so adjacent 3, hypotenuse 5; opposite \(\sqrt{25 - 9} = 4\).
\(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} < \beta < 2\pi\) is quadrant 4, where tangent is NEGATIVE.
Substitute into the compound angle formula (careful with the signs).
Numerator: common denominator 24.
Divide: multiply by the reciprocal.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(\cos 5x-\cos 7x\)?
questions.hint: Write \(5x\) and \(7x\) as \(6x-x\) and \(6x+x\), expand both with the compound-angle formulae and subtract.

steps.explain: The angles \(5x\) and \(7x\) are each one \(x\) away from the middle angle \(6x\). Write \(5x=6x-x\) and \(7x=6x+x\).
Expand the first with \(\cos(A-B)=\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B\).
Expand the second with \(\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B\).
Subtract the second from the first (careful with the minus sign in front of the whole bracket).
The \(\cos 6x\cos x\) terms cancel and the two \(\sin 6x\sin x\) terms add.

Check with \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\): LHS \(=\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}-\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=0\); RHS \(=2\sin\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}=0\) ✓. Option A fails with \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\): \(2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}=0\) but LHS \(=\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12}-\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{12}=0.259+0.259\ne 0\).
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: Write the two angles as 6x minus x and 6x plus x, then use the compound-angle formulae.

questions.hint: Replace \(2\cos7x\sin5x\) by \(\sin12x-\sin2x\) (part (i)). The \(\sin12x\) cancels, leaving a simple equation in \(\sin2x\). Remember that \(0\le x\le2\pi\) means \(0\le2x\le4\pi\): TWO full turns.

steps.explain: Using part (i), \(2\cos7x\sin5x=\sin12x-\sin2x\). Substitute.
Cancel \(\sin12x\) from both sides and multiply by \(-1\).
Domain: \(0\le x\le2\pi\) means \(0\le2x\le4\pi\). \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) has solutions \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) in the first turn, and \(2\pi\) more in the second turn.
Divide each by 2.
Check \(x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\): \(\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{3}=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) ✓. Option B forgets the second turn; C solves \(\sin x=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) incorrectly with 4 values.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: The sin 12x terms cancel; 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π gives two turns for 2x.

steps.explain: From part (i), \(y=\sqrt{10}\cos(t+\alpha)\), where \(\tan\alpha=3\). The threshold becomes \(\cos(t+\alpha)\ge\cos\alpha\).
Cosine is at least \(\cos\alpha\) within \(\alpha\) radians of each full-turn angle \(2k\pi\).
Intersect these intervals with the requested domain. The interval around t = 0 contributes no values because t = 0 is excluded.
The endpoint 4π is included, while the endpoints at t = 0 are excluded. These are the two audible intervals.

questions.stem: Let \(g(x)=\sqrt{3}\sin x+\cos x=R\sin(x+\alpha)\). Sketch the graphs of \(y=\ln x\) (blue) and \(y=g(x)\) (orange) on the same number plane, showing clearly any point(s) of intersection. Which sketch is correct? (Red circles mark the intersections.)
questions.hint: \(y=g(x)=2\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\) is a sine wave of amplitude 2 and period \(2\pi\), shifted LEFT \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), starting at \(g(0)=1\). \(y=\ln x\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x=0\), passes through \((1,0)\) and rises slowly to \(1.99\) at \(x\approx7.3\). Use the table values.

steps.explain: From part (i), \(g(x)=2\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\): amplitude 2, period \(2\pi\), \(g(0)=1\), maximum 2 at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), zeros at \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6},\dots\), minimum \(-2\) at \(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\), next maximum at \(\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\approx7.33\).

\(\ln x\): asymptote \(x=0\) (the \(y\)-axis), \(\ln1=0\), \(\ln\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=0.96\), \(\ln\dfrac{14\pi}{6}=1.99\), \(\ln\dfrac{20\pi}{6}=2.35\): it increases slowly, always below the maximum 2 of \(g\) until \(x\approx7.4\).

Intersections: (1) on the first falling part of \(g\) (\(g\) drops from 2 to 0 while \(\ln x\) climbs to \(0.96\)). (2),(3): near the next maximum \(x=\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\), where \(g=2\) is just above \(\ln x=1.99\), so \(g\) rises above \(\ln x\) and then falls back below it.
Why not the others: B shifts the wave right (\(g(0)=-1\)); C has amplitude 1; D plots \(\ln(x+1)\) (passes through the origin, no asymptote at \(x=0\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Let \(g(x)=\sqrt{3}\sin x+\cos x=R\sin(x+\alpha)\). Hence, determine the number of solutions to the equation \(\sqrt{3}\sin x+\cos x=\ln x\) in the domain \((0,\infty)\).
questions.hint: Solutions of \(g(x)=\ln x\) are the \(x\)-values where the two graphs intersect. Count the intersections, remembering that \(\ln x\) keeps climbing slowly but \(g\) never exceeds 2.

steps.explain: Where do the graphs meet? Around \(x\in\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\) (first crossing, \(g\) falling from 2 through \(\ln x\)).
Between \(x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and about \(7\) the wave is below \(\ln x\) (e.g. \(g\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)=-2<1.43\)), so no solutions.

Near the next maximum, \(g\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\right)=2>\ln\dfrac{7\pi}{3}=1.99\), so \(g\) pokes just above \(\ln x\): it crosses \(\ln x\) going up (table values at \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) and \(\dfrac{14\pi}{6}\)) and again going down (between \(\dfrac{14\pi}{6}\) and \(\dfrac{17\pi}{6}\)): 2 solutions.
Beyond that, \(\ln x>2\ge g(x)\) (since \(\ln x>2\) for \(x>e^{2}\approx7.39\)), so there are no more intersections.
Answer: 3 solutions.
So the correct choice is option C.
